t.1.8.1: But that great-souled king, so mighty and knowing what is right, though he practised austerities for the sake of a son, had no son to carry on his line.
t.1.8.2: As that great-souled one was reflecting thus, this thought arose in his mind: "Why do I not perform the horse sacrifice for the sake of a son?"
t.1.8.3: That wise and righteous-souled king, together with all his self-disciplined ministers, made a firm resolve, thinking, "A sacrifice must be performed."
t.1.8.4: Then the king said this to Sumantra, the best of ministers: "Quickly bring to me all those elders, together with the family priests."
t.1.8.6: O king, long ago the blessed Sanatkumāra told a story in the presence of the sages concerning the coming of your sons.
t.1.8.5: Having heard this, the charioteer spoke these words to the king in private: "I have heard this ancient account, as it was taught by the priests."
t.1.8.7: Kāśyapa has a son, renowned by the name Vibhāṇḍaka; to him will be born a son who will be famed as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
t.1.8.8: That sage, ever raised in the forest and always a forest-dweller, that foremost of brahmins, knows no one else, since he constantly follows only his father.
t.1.8.9: O king, the brahmacarya of that great-souled one will be twofold, a thing renowned throughout the worlds and always spoken of by the brahmins.
t.1.8.10: As he lived in this way, tending the sacred fire and serving his illustrious father, time passed on.
t.1.8.11: At this very time, the majestic and mighty Romapāda will be a renowned king among the Aṅgas.
t.1.8.12: Through that king's transgression there will come a most cruel and terrible drought, bringing fear to all living beings.
t.1.8.13: But when the drought has come about, the king, filled with sorrow, will summon the brāhmaṇas and those advanced in sacred learning, and will speak to them.
t.1.8.14: You, sirs, who are learned in dharma and know proper conduct in the world, prescribe the observance so that there may be expiation.
t.1.8.15: Those brāhmaṇas, masters of the Vedas, will say to the king: 'O king, bring the son of Vibhāṇḍaka here by every possible means.'
t.1.8.17: Hearing their words, the king will fall to pondering: by what means can that mighty one be brought here?
t.1.8.16: Having had Ṛṣyaśṛṅga brought to the king and well honoured, give him your daughter Śāntā according to the prescribed rite, with your mind fully composed.
t.1.8.18: Then the self-possessed king, having come to a decision together with his counsellors, will send forth his family priest and his ministers, duly honoured.
t.1.8.19: But they, hearing the king's words, were distressed and hung their heads: "Afraid of the sage, we would not go," and so they will try to win that king over.
t.1.8.20: Having reflected, they will declare suitable means for bringing him: "We shall bring the brahmin, and no fault will arise."
t.1.8.21: Thus the sage's son was brought by the lord of Aṅga himself by means of courtesans, the god sent down rain, and Śāntā is given to him.
t.1.8.23: Then Daśaratha, delighted, replied to Sumantra: "Let it be told by you in full how Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was brought here."
t.1.8.22: Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the son-in-law, will bring about sons for you. This much, as told by Sanatkumāra, has been related by me.
